data.name: Ishat
data.gender_notes: Ishat is used as a unisex name in Islamic naming traditions.
data.long_meaning: Derived from the Arabic root shata, meaning 'to give.' In Islamic tradition, Ishat is a name signifying the bestowal of blessings and favors from Allah. It is also the name of a companion of the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh), known for his generosity and kindness. The name Ishat carries the meaning “Gift, Grace” and is chosen by families in Islamic traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Arabic tradition and is also used in Arabic, Urdu, Persian. Parents who choose Ishat usually hope their child will grow to embody gift, grace and live with faith, good character and purpose.
data.etymology: Ishat belongs to the Arabic linguistic tradition and is used in Islamic naming. Its recorded meaning is “Gift, Grace.”
data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Ishat total 3, giving a life-path number of 3. Number 3 is linked with Jupiter and with the qualities of creativity, expression and optimism.

in_urdu.name: ایشات
in_urdu.meaning: عربی मूल کا نام جس کا مطلب ہے خواہش یا رغبت

historical_references.reference: Ishat bint Harb was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad and one of the earliest converts to Islam. She was the sister of Sa'd ibn Harb, who was a prominent leader in the early Islamic community. Ishat is believed to have been born in Mecca and was the wife of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, a close companion and scribe of the Prophet Muhammad. She is also known for her role in the Battle of the Camel, where she was among the women who rode out to support 'Ali ibn Abi Talib against Aisha and Talha. This battle took place in 656 CE during the First Fitna.

Ishat bint Nizam al-Masluki is another historical figure with the same name. She was a prominent Sufi saint and scholar in the Islamic world during the Abbasid Caliphate. Born in Baghdad around 850 CE, she was known for her piety, asceticism, and learning. She was a disciple of the Sufi master Junayd al-Baghdadi and was a teacher to many prominent Sufis, including 'Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani. Ishat is also known for her writings on Sufism and Islamic jurisprudence. Her most famous work is a commentary on Imam Ali's Sermon on the Day of Ghadir, which is considered a seminal text in Shia Islam.
